article-179.x: Illegal use of uniforms or insignia: publicly and improperly using insignia, uniforms or dress of an office not held, or of a class of persons of which one is not a member.
t: Use must be public and improper; an exact imitation is not required — a colorable resemblance that may deceive suffices.

article-180.x: False testimony against a defendant in a criminal case; the penalty depends on the sentence imposed on the defendant.
k: A criminal proceeding.
Testimony against the defendant.
The witness knows it is false.
The defendant is either convicted or acquitted in a final judgment.
t: The defendant must at least be sentenced (or acquitted) by final judgment before prosecution; the penalty varies by the sentence.

article-181.x: False testimony in favor of the defendant in a criminal case.
t: The false testimony need not actually benefit the defendant; it is enough that it was given to favor him.

article-182.x: False testimony in civil cases; the penalty depends on the amount in controversy.
t: The testimony must relate to the issues and be judicially given in a civil case.

article-183.x: Perjury (as amended by RA 11594, 2021): knowingly making untruthful statements under oath, or in an affidavit, on a material matter, before a competent person authorized to administer oaths, in cases where the law requires the oath. Solemn affirmations are covered. Public officers suffer the maximum period; all offenders also suffer a fine of up to ₱1,000,000 and perpetual absolute disqualification.
k: A statement under oath or an affidavit on a material matter.
Made before a competent officer authorized to administer oaths.
A willful and deliberate assertion of a falsehood.
The sworn statement is required by law or made for a legal purpose.
t: Good faith or a lack of malice is a defense: the falsehood must be willful and deliberate.
RA 11594 raised the penalty to prisión mayor in its minimum period; earlier cases cite the old, lighter penalty.

article-184.x: Offering false testimony in evidence: willfully and knowingly presenting a false witness or testimony in a judicial or official proceeding (as amended by RA 11594).
t: The offender is the one who offers the false witness, not the witness himself (who is liable under Arts. 180-183).

article-185.x: Machinations in public auctions: soliciting a gift or promise to stay out of a public auction; or attempting to keep bidders away by threats, gifts, promises or other artifices, to cause a reduction of the price.

article-186.x: Monopolies and combinations in restraint of trade — repealed by the Philippine Competition Act (RA 10667, 2015). Learn the Competition Act instead.

article-187.x: Importing, selling or disposing of articles of gold, silver or other precious metals falsely marked as to quality or fineness.

article-188.x: Substituting and altering trademarks and trade names — repealed by the Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293), which now punishes trademark infringement and unfair competition.

article-189.x: Unfair competition and fraudulent registration of trademarks — repealed by the Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293).

article-190.x: Part of the former Title Five on opium and prohibited drugs — repealed by RA 6425 (1972). Drug offenses are now governed by RA 9165 (2002), as amended.

article-191.x: Part of the former Title Five on opium and prohibited drugs — repealed by RA 6425 (1972). Drug offenses are now governed by RA 9165 (2002), as amended.

article-192.x: Part of the former Title Five on opium and prohibited drugs — repealed by RA 6425 (1972). Drug offenses are now governed by RA 9165 (2002), as amended.

article-193.x: Part of the former Title Five on opium and prohibited drugs — repealed by RA 6425 (1972). Drug offenses are now governed by RA 9165 (2002), as amended.

article-194.x: Part of the former Title Five on opium and prohibited drugs — repealed by RA 6425 (1972). Drug offenses are now governed by RA 9165 (2002), as amended.

article-195.x: Part of the Code’s gambling provisions (Arts. 195-199), repealed insofar as inconsistent by PD 1602 (1978). Illegal gambling is now punished under PD 1602, as amended by RA 9287 (illegal numbers games).

article-196.x: Part of the Code’s gambling provisions (Arts. 195-199), repealed insofar as inconsistent by PD 1602 (1978). Illegal gambling is now punished under PD 1602, as amended by RA 9287 (illegal numbers games).

article-198.x: Part of the Code’s gambling provisions (Arts. 195-199), repealed insofar as inconsistent by PD 1602 (1978). Illegal gambling is now punished under PD 1602, as amended by RA 9287 (illegal numbers games).

article-199.x: Part of the Code’s gambling provisions (Arts. 195-199), repealed insofar as inconsistent by PD 1602 (1978). Illegal gambling is now punished under PD 1602, as amended by RA 9287 (illegal numbers games).

article-197.x: Betting on sports contests — repealed by PD 483 (1974), which punishes betting, game-fixing and point-shaving in sports; see also PD 1602.

article-200.x: Grave scandal: highly scandalous conduct offending decency or good customs, not falling under any other article.
k: The act is highly scandalous, offending decency or good customs.
It is done publicly or comes to public knowledge.
It does not fall under any other article of the Code.
t: It is a residual crime: if the act is punished elsewhere (e.g., acts of lasciviousness, Art. 336), that article applies.

article-201.x: Immoral doctrines, obscene publications and exhibitions and indecent shows: publicly expounding doctrines contrary to public morals; authors, publishers and sellers of obscene literature; exhibitors of indecent or immoral plays or shows; and those who sell, give away or exhibit obscene films, prints and similar materials.
t: Obscenity is judged by contemporary community standards: whether the work, taken as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest and lacks serious value (the Court has drawn on Miller v. California).
Seizure of allegedly obscene materials requires a search warrant and a judicial determination of obscenity.

d.h: The warrantless seizure and burning of magazines by police as allegedly obscene was unconstitutional; obscenity must be determined by a court, and seizure requires a warrant issued on probable cause.
d.r: Procedure before suppressing materials as obscene.

d.h: The Court acknowledged that obscenity resists precise definition and is judged case by case under contemporary community standards; a store owner who sold pornographic materials was convicted under Art. 201.
d.r: Obscenity is a judicial question decided case by case.

article-202.x: Vagrants and prostitutes — repealed. RA 10158 (2012) decriminalized vagrancy, leaving only prostitution; RA 11862 (2022) then declared Art. 202 repealed. Trafficked persons are treated as victims under RA 9208, as amended.

article-203.x: Who are public officers for Book Two: any person who, by direct provision of law, popular election or appointment by competent authority, takes part in the performance of public functions in the Government, or performs public duties as an employee, agent or subordinate official, of any rank or class.
t: The definition is broad: what matters is participation in public functions, not rank or permanence of the position.

d.h: A private-sector representative appointed to the governing board of a government agency was a public officer for purposes of malversation and the anti-graft law: she performed public functions by appointment.

article-204.x: Knowingly rendering an unjust judgment: a judge renders a judgment that is unjust (contrary to law or unsupported by evidence), knowing it to be unjust.
k: Offender is a judge.
He renders a judgment in a case submitted to him.
The judgment is unjust.
He knows it is unjust.
t: A judge cannot be charged with knowingly rendering an unjust judgment while the judgment is pending review; there must first be a final declaration by a competent court that it is unjust (In re: Joaquin T. Borromeo).

d.h: A litigant who repeatedly filed criminal complaints against judges for “unjust” rulings was held in contempt; the proper remedy against an erroneous judgment is appeal or other judicial review, and a charge of knowingly rendering an unjust judgment requires a prior final finding that the judgment is unjust.

article-205.x: Unjust judgment through inexcusable negligence or ignorance: a judge who renders a manifestly unjust judgment by reason of inexcusable negligence or ignorance.

article-206.x: Unjust interlocutory order: a judge who knowingly — or through inexcusable negligence or ignorance — renders a manifestly unjust interlocutory order or decree.

article-207.x: Malicious delay in the administration of justice by a judge.
t: Delay alone is not enough; malice — a deliberate intent to prejudice a party — must be shown.

article-208.x: Prosecution of offenses; negligence and tolerance: a public officer or officer of the law who, in dereliction of duty, maliciously refrains from instituting prosecution for violations of law, or tolerates their commission.
t: The offender must have the duty to prosecute or move for prosecution (prosecutors, police officers, barangay officials with police functions).
If the officer refrains in exchange for a gift, see bribery (Arts. 210, 211-A).

article-209.x: Betrayal of trust by an attorney (or any person authorized to represent or assist a party): causing damage to a client by malicious breach of professional duty or inexcusable negligence or ignorance; revealing the client’s secrets learned in professional capacity; or, having undertaken a client’s defense, undertaking the defense of the opposing party in the same case without the first client’s consent.
t: Criminal liability is in addition to administrative (disciplinary) action under the CPRA.
Revealing secrets does not require damage; the first mode does.

article-210.x: Direct bribery (as amended by BP 871): a public officer who agrees to perform an act constituting a crime, or an act not constituting a crime, or refrains from doing something that is his official duty, in consideration of an offer, promise, gift or present received personally or through another. Applies also to assessors, arbitrators, appraisers, claim commissioners, experts and others performing public duties.
k: Offender is a public officer (or one performing public duties).
He accepts an offer or promise or receives a gift or present, personally or through another.
In consideration of: (1) committing a crime, (2) an unjust act not a crime, or (3) refraining from an official duty.
The act relates to the exercise of his functions.
t: In the first mode, the crime agreed upon is punished separately if committed.
The mere agreement in consideration of a gift received completes the first and third modes; for the second, the penalty depends on whether the act was executed.
The giver is liable for corruption of public officials (Art. 212).

i.s: Separately punishes corrupt practices of public officers (e.g., Sec. 3(e) undue injury or unwarranted benefits); a single act may violate both RA 3019 and the Code.

article-211.x: Indirect bribery (as amended by BP 871): a public officer who accepts gifts offered to him by reason of his office.
k: Offender is a public officer.
He accepts gifts.
The gifts are offered by reason of his office.
t: No agreement to do or not do an act is needed — that is the difference from direct bribery.
Acceptance is essential: a gift refused or immediately returned is not indirect bribery.
Indirect bribery cannot be committed in the attempted or frustrated stage.

article-211-a.x: Qualified bribery (added by RA 7659): a public officer entrusted with law enforcement who refrains from arresting or prosecuting an offender who committed a crime punishable by reclusion perpetua or death, in consideration of an offer, promise, gift or present, suffers the penalty for the offense not prosecuted; if he himself asked or demanded the gift, death (now reclusion perpetua without parole under RA 9346).

article-212.x: Corruption of public officials: the person who makes the offers or promises or gives the gifts or presents in Arts. 210, 211 and 211-A suffers the same penalties as the officer corrupted, except disqualification and suspension.
t: If the officer rejects the offer or promise, the giver may still be liable for attempted corruption of a public official.
Givers of bribes who testify against the public officer may be granted immunity under PD 749.

article-213.x: Frauds against the public treasury and illegal exactions: a public officer who, in his official capacity, enters into an agreement or uses another scheme to defraud the Government in dealings concerning public funds or property; and an officer in charge of collecting taxes or fees who demands sums different from or larger than those authorized, fails to issue receipts, or collects in kind without authority.
t: Illegal exaction by demanding a larger amount is consummated by the demand; actual collection is not required.
Mere demand of an amount larger than authorized may also violate RA 3019.

article-214.x: Other frauds: a public officer who, taking advantage of his position, commits any of the frauds in Chapter Six, Title Ten (estafa and other deceits) suffers, in addition, temporary special to perpetual special disqualification.
t: The estafa is still punished under Arts. 315-318; Art. 214 adds the disqualification.

article-215.x: Prohibited transactions: an appointive public officer who, during his incumbency, directly or indirectly becomes interested in a transaction of exchange or speculation within the territory subject to his jurisdiction.
t: Elective officials are not covered by Art. 215; see RA 6713 and RA 3019, Sec. 3(h).

article-216.x: Possession of prohibited interest: a public officer who, directly or indirectly, becomes interested in any contract or business in which he intervenes in his official capacity; also experts, arbitrators, guardians and executors as to property entrusted to them.
t: Actual fraud is not required; the conflict of interest itself is punished.

article-217.x: Malversation of public funds or property: a public officer accountable for public funds or property by reason of his duties who appropriates, takes or misappropriates them, consents to another’s taking, or through abandonment or negligence permits another to take them. The penalty depends on the amount (as adjusted by RA 10951). Failure to have the funds duly forthcoming upon demand by a duly authorized officer is prima facie evidence of personal use.
k: Offender is a public officer (or a private person under Art. 222, or one in conspiracy with the officer).
He has custody or control of funds or property by reason of his office.
They are public funds or property for which he is accountable.
He appropriated, took, misappropriated, or consented to or, through abandonment or negligence, permitted their taking.
t: Malversation may be committed intentionally or by negligence; the penalty is the same and an information for intentional malversation can support a conviction for malversation through negligence.
Demand is not an element; it only raises the presumption.
Restitution does not extinguish criminal liability; it may only mitigate.
Private individuals who conspire with the accountable officer are liable as co-principals.

i.s: Amassing ill-gotten wealth of at least ₱50 million through a combination or series of overt criminal acts (including malversation and bribery).

article-218.x: Failure of an accountable officer to render accounts: an accountable officer, in service or already separated, who fails to render his accounts to the Commission on Audit or a provincial auditor within two months after they should be rendered.
t: Misappropriation need not be shown.

article-219.x: Failure to render accounts before leaving the country: a public officer who unlawfully leaves or attempts to leave the Philippines without securing a certificate from the Commission on Audit that his accounts are fully settled.

article-220.x: Illegal use of public funds or property (technical malversation): a public officer who applies public funds or property under his administration to a public use other than that for which they were appropriated by law or ordinance. Heavier if damage or embarrassment to the public service results.
k: Public funds or property under his administration.
Appropriated by law or ordinance for a specific purpose.
Applied to another public use.
t: There is no personal gain: the funds go to a public purpose, just not the one appropriated. Good faith or that the new use was beneficial is no defense.

d.h: A mayor who diverted construction materials appropriated for a calamity-victims housing program to a different program was liable for technical malversation; criminal intent is not required, since the law punishes the unauthorized application itself.
d.r: Technical malversation is malum prohibitum in character.

article-221.x: Failure to make delivery of public funds or property: a public officer obliged to make a payment from Government funds in his possession who fails to do so, or who refuses to deliver property in his custody when ordered by competent authority.

article-222.x: The provisions on malversation apply to private individuals who have charge of public funds or property in any capacity, and to administrators or depositaries of funds or property attached, seized or deposited by public authority, even if owned by private individuals.
t: A private individual who, in conspiracy with an accountable officer, malversed funds is also liable (as a co-principal, not under Art. 222).

article-223.x: Conniving with or consenting to evasion: a public officer who consents to the escape of a prisoner in his custody or charge; the penalty depends on whether the prisoner was a convict or a detention prisoner.
t: The prisoner need not actually be convicted by final judgment for this article; “prisoner” includes detention prisoners.

article-224.x: Evasion through negligence: a public officer charged with the conveyance or custody of a prisoner who allows the escape through negligence.
t: The negligence must be definite and positive — not a mere lapse, such as when the escape was by force the officer could not prevent.

article-225.x: Escape of a prisoner in the custody of a private person: a private person to whom the conveyance or custody of a prisoner is entrusted who connives with, consents to, or through negligence allows the escape.

article-226.x: Removal, concealment or destruction of documents: a public officer who removes, destroys or conceals documents or papers officially entrusted to him, causing damage to a third party or the public interest.
t: Removal must be for an illicit purpose (e.g., to tamper with or profit from the document).

article-227.x: Officer breaking seal: a public officer charged with custody of papers or property sealed by proper authority who breaks the seals or permits them to be broken.
t: Damage is not required.

article-228.x: Opening of closed documents: a public officer, not covered by Art. 227, who opens or permits to be opened, without proper authority, closed papers, documents or objects entrusted to his custody.

article-229.x: Revelation of secrets by an officer: revealing secrets known to him by reason of his office, or wrongfully delivering papers or copies of papers he should not publish; heavier if serious damage to the public interest results.

article-230.x: Public officer revealing secrets of a private individual that he learned by reason of his office.

article-231.x: Open disobedience: a judicial or executive officer who openly refuses to execute the judgment, decision or order of a superior authority made within its jurisdiction and with the legal formalities.

article-232.x: Disobedience to an order of a superior that the inferior officer suspended: having suspended the order for any reason, the officer disobeys after the superior disapproves the suspension.

article-233.x: Refusal of assistance: a public officer who, upon demand from competent authority, fails to lend his cooperation toward the administration of justice or another public service; the penalty is heavier if the failure results in serious damage to the public interest or to a third party.

article-234.x: Refusal to discharge elective office: a person elected by popular election who refuses, without legal motive, to be sworn in or to discharge the duties of the office.

article-235.x: Maltreatment of prisoners: a public officer or employee who overdoes himself in the correction or handling of a prisoner or detention prisoner under his charge by imposing punishments not authorized by regulations, or by inflicting them in a cruel and humiliating manner; heavier if done to extort a confession or information.
t: The prisoner must be under the officer’s charge; otherwise the crime is physical injuries.
The Anti-Torture Act (RA 9745) separately punishes torture and is not absorbed by this article.

article-236.x: Anticipation of duties: assuming the duties and powers of a public office without first taking the oath or giving the required bond.

article-237.x: Prolonging performance of duties: a public officer who continues to exercise the duties of his office beyond the period provided by law, regulation or special provision.

article-238.x: Abandonment of office: a public officer who abandons his office before acceptance of his resignation, to the detriment of the public service; heavier if the purpose is to evade the discharge of duties of preventing, prosecuting or punishing crimes against national security.

article-239.x: Usurpation of legislative powers: a public officer who encroaches on legislative powers by making general rules or regulations beyond his authority, or attempts to repeal a law or suspend its execution.

article-240.x: Usurpation of executive functions: a judge who assumes a power pertaining to the executive authorities or obstructs them in the lawful exercise of their powers.

article-241.x: Usurpation of judicial functions: an officer of the executive branch who assumes judicial powers or obstructs the execution of an order or decision of a judge within his jurisdiction.

article-242.x: Disobeying a request for disqualification: a public officer who, before a question of jurisdiction is decided, continues the proceeding after having been lawfully required to refrain.

article-243.x: Orders or requests by executive officers to a judicial authority: an executive officer who addresses an order or suggestion to a judicial authority concerning a case within the latter’s exclusive jurisdiction.

article-244.x: Unlawful appointments: a public officer who knowingly nominates or appoints to a public office a person lacking the legal qualifications.

article-245.x: Abuses against chastity: (1) a public officer who solicits or makes immoral or indecent advances to a woman interested in a matter pending before him for decision or report; (2) a warden or officer in charge of prisoners who solicits or makes such advances to a woman under his custody; (3) the same advances to the wife, daughter, sister or relative within the same degree by affinity of a person in his custody.
t: Mere solicitation consummates the crime; the woman need not yield.
If the advances are accompanied by acts, other crimes (acts of lasciviousness, rape, sexual harassment under RA 7877 or RA 11313) may be committed.

article-246.x: Parricide: killing one’s father, mother or child (legitimate or illegitimate), any other legitimate ascendant or descendant, or one’s spouse.
k: A person is killed.
The accused killed him or her.
The deceased is the accused’s father, mother or child (legitimate or illegitimate), other legitimate ascendant or descendant, or legitimate spouse.
t: Only parents and children may be illegitimate; other ascendants and descendants must be legitimate. Killing an illegitimate grandchild is murder or homicide, not parricide.
The spouse must be a legitimate spouse — a void marriage means no parricide.
The relationship must be alleged in the information; otherwise it cannot qualify the killing.
A stranger who conspires with the relative is liable for murder or homicide, not parricide (relationship is personal).

i.s: Prohibits the imposition of the death penalty; reclusion perpetua is imposed instead, without eligibility for parole (and the crime is still called “qualified”).

article-247.x: Death or physical injuries under exceptional circumstances: a legally married person who surprises his spouse in the act of sexual intercourse with another and kills or seriously injures either or both in the act or immediately after suffers only destierro; less serious or slight injuries are exempt. The same applies to parents as to their daughters under eighteen living with them, and their seducers.
k: A legally married person (or a parent) surprises the spouse (or minor daughter) in the act of sexual intercourse.
He or she kills or inflicts serious physical injuries in the act or immediately thereafter.
He or she did not promote or facilitate the prostitution of the spouse or daughter, or consent to the infidelity.
t: Art. 247 does not define a crime; it grants a privilege and a near-exemption. Destierro is meant to protect the accused from retaliation, not to punish.
“Immediately thereafter” means the killing is the continuation of the act of discovery, without a break that allows reflection.
Third persons injured by stray shots: the accused may still be liable for the injuries to them through imprudence.

d.h: A husband who surprised his wife with her paramour, got a gun and shot the paramour within an hour was entitled to Art. 247; the article does not define a felony, and the injuries to bystanders were treated as less serious physical injuries through simple imprudence.

article-248.x: Murder: killing another (not parricide or infanticide) with any qualifying circumstance — treachery, abuse of superior strength, aid of armed men, means to weaken the defense or insure impunity; price, reward or promise; by inundation, fire, poison, explosion, shipwreck, derailment, attack on a vessel, motor vehicle or similar great waste and ruin; on the occasion of a calamity; evident premeditation; or cruelty, by deliberately augmenting the suffering of the victim or outraging or scoffing at his person or corpse.
k: A person was killed.
The accused killed him.
With at least one qualifying circumstance of Art. 248.
Not parricide or infanticide.
t: Treachery: (1) means of execution that gave the person attacked no opportunity to defend himself; (2) deliberately or consciously adopted. A sudden attack is not treachery if it was not deliberately chosen.
Only one qualifying circumstance is needed; others present become generic aggravating circumstances.
Qualifying circumstances must be alleged in the information (Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 110, Secs. 8-9).
Death in the text is now reclusion perpetua without parole (RA 9346).

i.s: Prohibits the imposition of the death penalty; reclusion perpetua is imposed instead, without eligibility for parole (and the crime is still called “qualified”).

article-249.x: Homicide: killing another without any of the circumstances of murder, and not parricide or infanticide.
t: Intent to kill is presumed from the fact of death; for frustrated or attempted homicide it must be proven (e.g., from the weapon used, the wounds, the words uttered).

article-250.x: For frustrated parricide, murder or homicide, the court may impose a penalty one degree lower than that for the frustrated felony, and for attempted, two degrees lower than that for the attempt.
t: This is discretionary (“may”).

article-251.x: Death in a tumultuous affray: several persons, not organized into groups, quarrel and assault one another in a confused and tumultuous manner; someone is killed; and it cannot be ascertained who killed him. Those who inflicted serious physical injuries are punished; if they cannot be identified, all who used violence on the victim.
k: Several persons, not composing groups organized to attack each other.
They quarrel and assault each other in a confused and tumultuous manner.
Someone is killed in the course of the affray.
The killer cannot be identified.
It can be determined who inflicted serious physical injuries or who used violence.
t: If the killer is identified, he is liable for homicide or murder; Art. 251 applies only when he cannot be identified.
If the participants were organized groups, the crime is homicide or murder (conspiracy).

article-252.x: Physical injuries in a tumultuous affray: only serious (or less serious) physical injuries are inflicted on participants and the person responsible cannot be identified; all who used violence on the injured party are punished.

article-253.x: Giving assistance to suicide: assisting another to commit suicide; heavier if the assistance extends to doing the killing oneself. If the suicide is not consummated, a lower penalty applies.
t: A person who attempts suicide is not punished.
Euthanasia (mercy killing by a third person) is homicide or murder in Philippine law, not assistance to suicide, unless the person merely helped the patient kill himself.

article-254.x: Discharge of firearms (as amended by RA 11926): (a) shooting at another with a firearm, without intent to kill, unless the facts constitute frustrated or attempted parricide, murder, homicide or a heavier crime; (b) wilful and indiscriminate discharge of any firearm or device usable as one; (c) one degree higher for military or law-enforcement personnel not on duty. The offender’s firearm license is cancelled and he is perpetually disqualified from holding one.
t: For (a), the firearm must be aimed at the victim; firing into the air near someone is not “shooting at another” (it may be (b)).
If intent to kill is shown, the crime is attempted or frustrated homicide or murder.

article-255.x: Infanticide: killing a child less than three days old. The penalty is that for parricide or murder; if committed by the mother to conceal her dishonor, or by maternal grandparents for the same purpose, a lower penalty applies.
t: If the child is three days old or more, the crime is parricide (if by a parent) or murder.
The child must have been born alive and capable of independent life; killing a fetus is abortion.
Concealing dishonor benefits only the mother and the maternal grandparents.

article-256.x: Intentional abortion: (1) by violence on the pregnant woman; (2) without violence and without her consent; (3) with her consent.
k: A pregnant woman.
Violence or drugs or other means are used to cause the abortion.
The fetus dies, in the womb or after expulsion.
The abortion is intended.
t: If the fetus is expelled alive and capable of independent life and then killed, the crime is infanticide or murder.

article-257.x: Unintentional abortion: abortion caused by violence on a pregnant woman, without intent to cause it.
t: The offender must know of the pregnancy, or it must be visible, and must have used violence; if the woman is also killed, it is a complex crime (Art. 48).

article-258.x: Abortion practiced by the woman herself, or by her parents with her consent; lower penalties if she acted to conceal her dishonor.

article-259.x: Abortion practiced by a physician or midwife, and dispensing of abortives by a pharmacist without a proper prescription.

article-260.x: Killing or injuring an adversary in a duel; seconds are punished as accomplices.

article-261.x: Challenging another to a duel, inciting another to give or accept a challenge, or publicly scoffing at a person for refusing a challenge.

article-262.x: Mutilation: (1) intentionally depriving another, totally or partially, of an essential organ for reproduction (castration); (2) any other intentional mutilation, by lopping or clipping off any part of the body.
t: Mutilation requires intent to deprive the victim of the body part; an injury that results in loss of a body part without that intent is serious physical injuries.

d.h: A vasectomy performed on a mentally impaired man at his guardian’s instance was not mutilation: there was no malicious intent to deprive him of an organ for reproduction, and the procedure did not remove the organ.

article-263.x: Serious physical injuries, graded by the result: insanity, imbecility, impotence or blindness; loss of speech, hearing, smell, an eye, a hand, foot, arm or leg, or the use of any of them, or incapacity for the work habitually engaged in; deformity, loss of another part of the body, or incapacity for labor for more than ninety days; illness or incapacity for labor for more than thirty days. Heavier if against relatives listed in Art. 246 or with the circumstances of murder.
t: There is no intent to kill; if there is, the crime is attempted or frustrated homicide or murder.
Deformity requires a visible and permanent physical ugliness (e.g., loss of front teeth may qualify).

article-264.x: Administering injurious substances or beverages: knowingly administering an injurious substance, or taking advantage of the victim’s weakness of mind or credulity, causing serious physical injuries, without intent to kill.

article-265.x: Less serious physical injuries: injuries that incapacitate the victim for labor for ten days or more (but not more than thirty), or require medical assistance for the same period; heavier if there was manifest intent to insult or offend, or circumstances adding ignominy, or against persons in authority or relatives.

article-266.x: Slight physical injuries and maltreatment: injuries incapacitating the victim for one to nine days, or requiring medical assistance for that period; injuries not preventing work and not requiring medical assistance; and ill-treatment by deed without causing injury.
t: Ill-treatment without injury (a slap) may instead be slander by deed (Art. 359) if done to dishonor.

article-266-b.x: Penalties for rape. Rape by sexual intercourse: reclusion perpetua; reclusion perpetua to death with a deadly weapon or by two or more persons, or when the victim becomes insane, or attempted rape with homicide. Death (now reclusion perpetua without parole) for rape with homicide and for qualified rape — e.g., victim under eighteen and offender a parent, ascendant, step-parent, guardian, relative within the third civil degree, or common-law spouse of the parent; victim under seven; offender knew of the victim’s mental disability; and the other circumstances listed. Rape by sexual assault: prision mayor, higher when qualified.
t: Qualifying circumstances (minority plus relationship, for example) must be alleged and proved; otherwise the rape is simple.
Rape with homicide is a special complex crime: all killings on the occasion of the rape are merged into it.
Under RA 9346 the penalty is reclusion perpetua, but the offense is still designated as qualified rape and is not eligible for parole.

i.s: Prohibits the imposition of the death penalty; reclusion perpetua is imposed instead, without eligibility for parole (and the crime is still called “qualified”).

article-266-c.x: Effect of pardon: the subsequent valid marriage between the offender and the offended party extinguishes the criminal action or the penalty. Where the legal husband is the offender, the wife’s subsequent forgiveness extinguishes the action or penalty, unless the marriage is void ab initio.
t: Marital rape is a crime (the husband can be the offender), and the wife’s forgiveness extinguishes it.
In multiple-offender rape, marriage to one offender extinguishes only that offender’s liability.

article-266-d.x: Presumptions: any physical overt act manifesting resistance, in any degree, or circumstances that render the victim incapable of giving valid consent, may be accepted as evidence of rape by sexual intercourse.
t: Resistance is not an element of rape; it is only evidence of lack of consent. A victim frozen by fear need not resist.

article-267.x: Kidnapping and serious illegal detention (as amended by RA 7659): a private individual who kidnaps or detains another, or deprives him of liberty, when (1) the detention lasts more than three days; (2) it is committed simulating public authority; (3) serious physical injuries are inflicted or threats to kill are made; or (4) the person kidnapped is a minor (except when the accused is a parent), a female or a public officer. Death (now reclusion perpetua without parole) when committed to extort ransom, even if none of those circumstances is present; and when the victim is killed or dies, or is raped, or subjected to torture or dehumanizing acts.
k: Offender is a private individual.
He kidnaps or detains another, or deprives him of liberty.
The detention is illegal.
Any of the four circumstances, or the purpose of extorting ransom.
t: For kidnapping for ransom, actual payment is not required; the purpose is enough.
When the victim is killed, raped, tortured or subjected to dehumanizing acts, it is a special complex crime (kidnapping with homicide, rape, etc.) — RA 7659’s last paragraph.
If the primary intent was to kill and the detention was only incidental, the crime is murder, not kidnapping.
A public officer who detains without legal ground commits arbitrary detention (Art. 124), unless he acts in a private capacity.

d.h: The abduction and killing of two sisters were special complex crimes of kidnapping and serious illegal detention with homicide and rape under the last paragraph of Art. 267 as amended by RA 7659; where the victim is killed in the course of the detention, the crimes are not complexed under Art. 48 but form one special complex crime.

i.s: Prohibits the imposition of the death penalty; reclusion perpetua without eligibility for parole is imposed instead.

article-268.x: Slight illegal detention: kidnapping or detention without any of the circumstances of Art. 267. A lower penalty applies if the offender voluntarily releases the victim within three days without attaining his purpose and before criminal proceedings begin.
t: The voluntary release is a privileged mitigating circumstance; all three conditions must be present.

article-269.x: Unlawful arrest: arresting or detaining another to deliver him to the proper authorities, in a case not authorized by law or without reasonable ground.
t: The purpose is delivery to the authorities; if the purpose is otherwise, the crime is illegal detention.

article-270.x: Kidnapping and failure to return a minor: a person entrusted with the custody of a minor who deliberately fails to restore him to his parents or guardians.
t: The essential element is the deliberate failure to restore the minor; the custody itself may have begun lawfully (e.g., a nanny or a relative).

article-271.x: Inducing a minor to abandon his home, or the home of his parents or guardians; lighter if committed by the father or mother.

article-272.x: Slavery: purchasing, selling, kidnapping or detaining a human being to enslave him; heavier if for assigning him to immoral traffic.
t: Trafficking in persons is now punished more broadly by RA 9208, as amended.

article-273.x: Exploitation of child labor: under pretext of reimbursing a debt incurred by the minor’s ascendant, guardian or custodian, retaining the minor in one’s service against his will.

article-274.x: Services rendered under compulsion in payment of debts: compelling a debtor to work for the creditor, against his will, as household servant or farm laborer.

article-275.x: Abandonment of persons in danger: failing to help a person found wounded or in danger of dying in an uninhabited place, when one can do so without detriment to oneself; failing to help one’s own victim of an accident; and failing to deliver a child under seven found abandoned to its family or the authorities.
t: In item 2 the accident must be caused by the offender without fault; if by his fault, see Art. 365 (failure to render aid aggravates reckless imprudence).

article-276.x: Abandoning a minor under seven whose custody is incumbent on the offender; heavier if the child dies or his life is endangered. Parents who relinquish an infant thirty days old or younger to a safe haven are exempt (RA 11767).

article-277.x: Abandonment of a minor by the person entrusted with his custody (delivering him to a public institution or others without consent), and indifference of parents (neglecting to educate children as their station and financial condition permit).

article-278.x: Exploitation of minors: making a child under sixteen perform dangerous feats of balancing, physical strength or contortion; employing children as acrobats or in similar callings; and delivering a child to such persons. The child-labor laws (RA 9231) also apply.

article-279.x: The penalties for the preceding articles do not prevent the imposition of penalties for other felonies committed.

article-280.x: Qualified trespass to dwelling: a private person who enters the dwelling of another against the latter’s will; heavier if by violence or intimidation. Not applicable to entering to prevent serious harm, to render service to humanity or justice, or entering cafes, taverns and public houses while open.
k: Offender is a private person.
He enters the dwelling of another.
Against the will of the owner (express or implied prohibition).
t: “Against the will” requires a prohibition; mere lack of consent is not enough, but entering through a closed door at night implies prohibition.
A public officer who does this commits violation of domicile (Art. 128).

article-281.x: Other forms of trespass: entering closed premises or fenced estates of another while uninhabited, when the prohibition to enter is manifest and the trespasser has not secured the owner’s permission.

article-282.x: Grave threats: threatening another with a wrong amounting to a crime against his person, honor or property or that of his family — (1) with a demand for money or another condition, attained or not; (2) without a condition.
t: Threats in writing or through a middleman get the maximum period.
If the threat is made with a weapon in the heat of anger, see Art. 285.

article-283.x: Light threats: threatening a wrong not constituting a crime, with a demand for money or another condition.
t: Example: threatening to expose a person’s affair unless paid — the wrong (exposure) is not a crime, but the demand makes it light threats (and may be blackmail).

article-284.x: In cases of grave and light threats, the offender may be required to give bail not to molest the threatened person; or be sentenced to destierro if he fails to give it.

article-285.x: Other light threats: threatening with a weapon or drawing it in a quarrel (not in self-defense); orally threatening in the heat of anger a wrong amounting to a crime when the acts show no intent to carry it out; and threatening a wrong not amounting to a crime without demand.

article-286.x: Grave coercion: without authority of law, by violence, threats or intimidation, preventing another from doing something not prohibited by law, or compelling him to do something against his will, right or wrong. Heavier if in violation of the right of suffrage or to compel or prevent a religious act.
k: A person prevented from doing what is lawful, or compelled to do something against his will.
By violence, threats or intimidation.
Without authority of law.
t: If the act is punished by another article (e.g., robbery, kidnapping), that article applies; grave coercion is generic.

article-287.x: Light coercions: seizing by violence anything belonging to one’s debtor to apply it to the debt; and “any other coercions or unjust vexations” — any human conduct that unjustly annoys or irritates another without violence (unjust vexation).
t: Unjust vexation is the catch-all: the test is whether the act caused annoyance, irritation, torment or distress to the offended party.

article-288.x: Other similar coercions: forcing employees to buy merchandise from the employer, and paying wages in tokens or objects other than legal tender.

article-289.x: Using violence or threats to compel or force laborers or employers in organizing, maintaining or preventing coalitions, strikes or lockouts, if the act is not a more serious offense.

article-290.x: Discovering secrets by seizing another’s papers or letters and revealing their contents; lower penalty if not revealed. Not applicable to parents and guardians as to minors in their care, or spouses as to each other’s papers.
t: RA 4200 (Anti-Wiretapping Act) and RA 10173 (Data Privacy Act) separately protect communications and personal data.

article-291.x: Revealing secrets with abuse of office: a manager, employee or servant who learns secrets of his principal or master in that capacity and reveals them.

article-292.x: Revelation of industrial secrets: a person in charge, employee or workman of a manufacturing or industrial establishment who reveals its secrets to the prejudice of the owner.

article-293.x: Robbery: taking personal property belonging to another, with intent to gain, by means of violence against or intimidation of any person, or using force upon things.
k: Personal property belonging to another.
Unlawful taking (apoderamiento).
Intent to gain (animus lucrandi), presumed from the unlawful taking.
Violence against or intimidation of persons, or force upon things.
t: The violence or intimidation must be present before or at the time of the taking; violence used afterward to keep the loot may still be robbery if done to effect the taking.
Taking a motor vehicle is carnapping (RA 10883).

i.s: Taking a motor vehicle is carnapping, punished under this special law rather than as theft or robbery.

article-294.x: Robbery with violence against or intimidation of persons (as amended by RA 7659): graded penalties for (1) robbery with homicide (or rape, intentional mutilation or arson); (2) with serious physical injuries causing insanity, imbecility, impotency or blindness; (3) with other serious physical injuries; (4) with unnecessary violence or injuries beyond what the robbery required; (5) other cases.
t: Robbery with homicide: the intent is to rob, and the killing is by reason or on occasion of it. “Homicide” is used in its generic sense — all killings, including of robbers, merge into one special complex crime.
If the original intent was to kill and the taking was an afterthought, the crimes are homicide/murder and theft, separately.

d.h: In robbery with homicide the original criminal design is robbery and the killing is committed by reason or on occasion of it; “homicide” is used in its generic sense and absorbs all killings and injuries on that occasion.

i.s: Prohibits the imposition of the death penalty; reclusion perpetua without eligibility for parole is imposed instead.

article-295.x: Robbery with physical injuries in an uninhabited place or by a band, or with the use of a firearm on a street, road, highway or alley (as amended by RA 12 and RA 373): the offender suffers the maximum period of the penalty for robbery under subdivisions 3, 4 and 5 of Art. 294; the leader of the band, the penalty next higher in degree.

article-296.x: Definition of a band: more than three armed malefactors taking part in a robbery. If any arm used is an unlicensed firearm, all suffer the maximum penalty. Any member of the band present at the robbery is liable as principal for the assaults committed by the band, unless he tried to prevent them.
t: “More than three” means at least four, all armed.

article-297.x: Attempted or frustrated robbery with homicide: a special complex crime with its own penalty.
t: The robbery may be attempted or frustrated, but the homicide must be consummated.

article-298.x: Execution of deeds by means of violence or intimidation: compelling another, with intent to defraud, to sign, execute or deliver a public instrument or document.

article-299.x: Robbery in an inhabited house, public building or edifice devoted to worship, by armed persons, by entering (through an opening not intended for entrance, breaking walls, roofs, floors, doors or windows, using false keys or picklocks, or under pretense of public authority), or, once inside, by breaking locked or sealed furniture or receptacles or taking them away to be broken outside. Penalty depends on value and whether the offenders were armed.
t: The force upon things must be used to enter (or, once inside, to open locked receptacles); breaking out to escape is not this robbery.

article-300.x: Robbery in an inhabited house in an uninhabited place and by a band: maximum period of the penalty.

article-301.x: Definitions: an inhabited house is any shelter, ship or vessel that is the dwelling of one or more persons, even if temporarily absent; dependencies are interior courts, corrals, warehouses and other places contiguous to the building with an interior entrance.

article-302.x: Robbery in an uninhabited place or in a private building by any of the means of force upon things; heavier for mail matter or large cattle.

article-303.x: Robbery of cereals, fruits or firewood in the cases of Arts. 299 and 302: one degree lower.

article-304.x: Possession of picklocks or similar tools specially adapted to robbery, without lawful cause; heavier for locksmiths who make them.

article-305.x: False keys: the tools in Art. 304, genuine keys stolen from the owner, and any keys other than those intended by the owner for use in the lock forcibly opened.

article-306.x: Brigandage (as amended by RA 12): more than three armed persons forming a band of robbers to commit robbery in the highway, kidnapping for extortion or ransom, or any other purpose by force and violence. Use of an unlicensed firearm raises a presumption of brigandage.
t: Brigandage is consummated by the formation of the band for those purposes; no robbery need be committed.
Compare PD 532 (highway robbery): applies to indiscriminate robbery of travelers; People v. Puno (1993).

article-307.x: Aiding and abetting a band of brigands: knowingly aiding, abetting or protecting it, giving it information, or acquiring or receiving property taken by it. Aid is presumed knowing unless the contrary is proven.

article-308.x: Theft: taking personal property of another with intent to gain, without violence, intimidation or force upon things, and without the owner’s consent. Also theft: failing to deliver lost property found to the owner or authorities; damaging another’s property and removing or using the fruits; and entering an enclosed estate or field to hunt, fish or gather fruits without consent.
k: Taking of personal property.
Belonging to another.
With intent to gain.
Without the owner’s consent.
Without violence, intimidation or force upon things.
t: There is no frustrated theft: theft is consummated once the offender has taken the property with intent to gain, even if he could not dispose of it (Valenzuela v. People).
The finder who keeps lost property commits theft even without knowing who the owner is.
“Taking” requires unlawful deprivation of possession; juridical possession received from the owner (e.g., as agent) makes the misappropriation estafa, not theft.

d.h: Theft is consummated upon the taking of the property with intent to gain; the ability to freely dispose of it is not an element. There is no frustrated theft.

article-309.x: Penalties for theft by value of the thing stolen (adjusted by RA 10951 in 2017).
t: Use the RA 10951 brackets for crimes committed after it took effect, and also for earlier ones where it is favorable to the accused (Art. 22).

article-310.x: Qualified theft (as amended by RA 120 and BP 71): theft punished two degrees higher if committed by a domestic servant, with grave abuse of confidence, or if the property is a motor vehicle, mail matter or large cattle, coconuts from a plantation, fish from a fishpond, or property taken on the occasion of fire, earthquake, typhoon, volcanic eruption or other calamity, vehicular accident or civil disturbance.
t: Grave abuse of confidence requires a relation of trust that facilitated the taking (e.g., a bank teller).
Motor vehicles are now covered by the Anti-Carnapping Act (RA 10883) and large cattle by PD 533.

d.h: A bank cash custodian who received money only in material (physical) possession, the bank keeping juridical possession, could not be convicted of estafa for the missing money; the proper charge was theft (qualified theft).
d.r: Material vs. juridical possession — theft or estafa.

i.s: Taking a motor vehicle is carnapping, punished under this special law rather than as theft or robbery.

article-311.x: Theft of property of the National Library or National Museum: penalty of arresto mayor or a fine, or both, unless a higher penalty applies under other provisions.

article-312.x: Occupation of real property or usurpation of real rights: taking possession of real property or usurping a real right of another by violence or intimidation; a fine based on the gain is added to the penalty for the violence.
t: Violence or intimidation is essential; peaceful but unlawful occupation is not this crime (civil remedies or anti-squatting rules apply).

article-313.x: Altering boundaries or landmarks of towns, provinces or estates, or any marks intended to designate them.

article-314.x: Fraudulent insolvency: absconding with one’s property to the prejudice of creditors; heavier if the offender is a merchant.

article-315.x: Estafa (swindling), penalties by amount (adjusted by RA 10951). Three groups of means: (1) with unfaithfulness or abuse of confidence — altering the substance, quantity or quality of things delivered; misappropriating or converting money or goods received in trust, on commission, for administration, or under any obligation to deliver or return; taking undue advantage of a signature in blank; (2) by false pretenses or fraudulent acts executed prior to or simultaneously with the fraud — e.g., pretending to possess power, qualifications or property; postdating or issuing a check without funds (par. 2(d)); (3) through other fraudulent means (e.g., inducing another to sign a document by deceit, removing documents from court records).
k: Abuse of confidence (par. 1(b)): money or property received in trust or under an obligation to return; misappropriation or conversion or denial of receipt; prejudice to another; demand (evidence of misappropriation, not an element).
Deceit (par. 2): false pretense made before or at the time of the fraud; reliance on it; damage.
Par. 2(d): failure to fund the check within three days of notice of dishonor is prima facie evidence of deceit.
t: Estafa needs damage or prejudice; BP 22 does not. One check may give rise to both offenses.
In par. 1(b) the offender must have received juridical possession; if only material possession, the crime is theft (Chua-Burce v. CA).
Syndicated estafa (five or more, defrauding the public of funds solicited from the public) is punished by PD 1689.

i.s: Issuing a check that bounces is punished regardless of deceit or damage; estafa under Art. 315(2)(d) requires deceit and damage. One act may give rise to both.

article-316.x: Other forms of swindling: pretending to be the owner of real property and disposing of it; disposing of encumbered real property as free; wrongfully taking personal property from its lawful possessor (owner’s case); executing a fictitious contract to another’s prejudice; accepting compensation for services not rendered; and selling, mortgaging or encumbering real property given as surety.

article-317.x: Swindling a minor: taking advantage of a minor’s inexperience or emotions to make him assume an obligation, give a release, or execute a transfer of property right, to his detriment.

article-318.x: Other deceits not covered by the preceding articles; and interpreting dreams, making forecasts, telling fortunes, or taking advantage of public credulity for profit.

article-319.x: Removal, sale or pledge of mortgaged property: knowingly removing personal property mortgaged under the Chattel Mortgage Law to another province or city without the mortgagee’s written consent; or selling or pledging it without the mortgagee’s written consent noted on the record of mortgage.

article-320.x: Destructive arson (as amended by RA 7659): burning one or more buildings or edifices in a single act or several acts; buildings for public use or where people assemble; trains, ships, airplanes or vehicles for transport of persons or property; public buildings or archives; arsenals, factories and the like; and other listed properties. If death results, death (now reclusion perpetua without parole).
t: Arson other than destructive arson is punished under PD 1613.
If the intent was to kill and fire was the means, the crime is murder (by means of fire), not arson.

i.s: Punishes simple arson and its kinds; destructive arson remains in Art. 320 as amended by RA 7659.
Prohibits the imposition of the death penalty; reclusion perpetua without eligibility for parole is imposed instead.

article-321.x: Part of the Code’s original arson provisions (Arts. 321-326-B), superseded by PD 1613 (1979). Learn PD 1613 and Art. 320 as amended by RA 7659 instead.

article-322.x: Part of the Code’s original arson provisions (Arts. 321-326-B), superseded by PD 1613 (1979). Learn PD 1613 and Art. 320 as amended by RA 7659 instead.

article-323.x: Part of the Code’s original arson provisions (Arts. 321-326-B), superseded by PD 1613 (1979). Learn PD 1613 and Art. 320 as amended by RA 7659 instead.

article-324.x: Part of the Code’s original arson provisions (Arts. 321-326-B), superseded by PD 1613 (1979). Learn PD 1613 and Art. 320 as amended by RA 7659 instead.

article-325.x: Part of the Code’s original arson provisions (Arts. 321-326-B), superseded by PD 1613 (1979). Learn PD 1613 and Art. 320 as amended by RA 7659 instead.

article-326.x: Part of the Code’s original arson provisions (Arts. 321-326-B), superseded by PD 1613 (1979). Learn PD 1613 and Art. 320 as amended by RA 7659 instead.

article-327.x: Malicious mischief: deliberately causing damage to another’s property, not falling within arson.
k: Deliberate damage to another’s property.
Not constituting arson.
The act of damaging is done for its own sake (hate, revenge, or mere pleasure of destroying).
t: If the damage is caused to gain (e.g., destroying to take), the crime may be theft or robbery.

article-328.x: Special cases of malicious mischief: causing damage to obstruct public functions; using poisonous or corrosive substances; spreading infection among cattle; damage to public property or works of art.

article-329.x: Other mischiefs not included in Art. 328, penalized by the value of the damage.

article-330.x: Damage and obstruction to means of communication: damaging railway, telegraph or telephone lines; heavier if it endangers a train.

article-331.x: Destroying or damaging statues, public monuments or paintings.

article-332.x: Absolutory cause: no criminal, only civil, liability for theft, swindling or malicious mischief committed between spouses, ascendants and descendants or relatives by affinity in the same line; a widowed spouse as to property of the deceased spouse not yet passed to another; and brothers and sisters and brothers-in-law and sisters-in-law living together.
t: It covers only theft, swindling (estafa) and malicious mischief — not robbery, not estafa complexed with falsification (Intestate Estate of Gonzales vda. de Carungcong v. People, 2010).
Strangers who participate are not exempt.

d.n: Intestate Estate of Manolita Gonzales vda. de Carungcong v. People
d.h: A son-in-law accused of estafa through falsification against his mother-in-law could not invoke Art. 332: the absolutory cause covers simple estafa, not the complex crime of estafa through falsification of public documents, which also offends public interest. The relationship by affinity survives the death of the spouse for purposes of Art. 332.

article-333.x: Adultery: a married woman who has sexual intercourse with a man not her husband, and the man who knows she is married. Each act of intercourse is a separate adultery.
k: The woman is married (even if the marriage is later declared void).
She has sexual intercourse with a man not her husband.
The man knows she is married (as to his liability).
t: Only the offended husband can file the complaint, and he must include both guilty parties if both are alive (Art. 344).
Consent or pardon by the husband bars prosecution.
If the husband was abandoned without justification, the penalty is lower (par. 3).

article-334.x: Concubinage: a husband who (1) keeps a mistress in the conjugal dwelling; (2) has sexual intercourse with a woman not his wife under scandalous circumstances; or (3) cohabits with her in any other place. The concubine is punished with destierro.
t: Concubinage is harder to prove than adultery: a single act of intercourse is not enough unless under scandalous circumstances.
The same act may also be psychological violence under RA 9262 (marital infidelity causing mental anguish).

article-335.x: Old rape provision — repealed by RA 8353 (1997). Rape is now Arts. 266-A to 266-D.

article-336.x: Acts of lasciviousness: committing any act of lasciviousness on a person of either sex under any of the circumstances of rape (force or intimidation, deprivation of reason or unconsciousness, fraudulent machination or grave abuse of authority, or the victim’s age or dementia).
k: An act of lasciviousness or lewdness.
On another person of either sex.
Under any of the circumstances of rape (now Art. 266-A).
t: The difference from attempted rape is intent: acts that show intent to lie with the victim are attempted rape; lewd acts without that intent are acts of lasciviousness.
If the victim is a child exploited in prostitution or subjected to other sexual abuse, RA 7610, Sec. 5(b) applies with a heavier penalty (People v. Tulagan, 2019; Dimakuta v. People, 2015).

d.h: Where the victim is a child at least twelve but below eighteen and the act is lascivious conduct under RA 7610, the accused should be convicted under RA 7610, Sec. 5(b), which carries the heavier penalty, rather than under Art. 336.

i.t: Special Protection of Children Act (RA 7610), Sec. 5(b)
i.s: Lascivious conduct with a child exploited in prostitution or subjected to other sexual abuse carries a heavier penalty; see People v. Tulagan (2019) for when the Code or RA 7610 applies.

article-337.x: Qualified seduction (as amended by RA 11648): seduction of a minor sixteen and over but under eighteen by a person in public authority, priest, house-servant, domestic, guardian, teacher, or anyone entrusted with the minor’s education or custody; and seduction of one’s sister or descendant, whatever her age or reputation.
k: The victim is sixteen or over but under eighteen (since RA 11648).
The offender has carnal knowledge of her.
The offender abuses his authority, confidence or relationship (one of the listed persons).
t: Below sixteen, the act is statutory rape (Art. 266-A(1)(d)).
RA 11648 replaced “a virgin over twelve” with “a minor, sixteen and over but under eighteen”; virginity is no longer required in the text.
For a sister or descendant, age and virginity do not matter.

article-338.x: Simple seduction (as amended by RA 11648): seduction of a minor sixteen and over but under eighteen by means of deceit (typically an unfulfilled promise of marriage).

article-339.x: Acts of lasciviousness with the consent of the offended party: lascivious acts by the same persons and under the same circumstances as in qualified and simple seduction (Arts. 337 and 338).
t: Compare Art. 336 (without consent, under the circumstances of rape).

article-340.x: Corruption of minors (as amended by BP 92): promoting or facilitating the prostitution or corruption of persons under age to satisfy the lust of another; a public officer or employee (including in GOCCs) also suffers temporary absolute disqualification.
t: Since BP 92, habituality and abuse of authority are no longer required; a single act suffices.
It is the lust of another that must be satisfied; the offender who satisfies his own lust commits another crime.

article-341.x: White slave trade (as amended by BP 186): engaging in the business of prostitution, profiting by it, or enlisting the services of any other person for prostitution.
t: Trafficking for sexual exploitation is now mainly prosecuted under RA 9208 as amended, with much heavier penalties.

article-342.x: Forcible abduction: taking away a woman against her will and with lewd designs; the same penalty if she is under twelve, even if she consents.
k: The person abducted is a woman (of any age, civil status or reputation).
She is taken against her will.
With lewd designs.
t: If rape follows, the crime is forcible abduction with rape (complex crime, Art. 48) when the abduction was the means; later rapes are separate crimes.
If the purpose is not lewd, the crime may be kidnapping or grave coercion.

article-343.x: Consented abduction: abduction of a virgin over twelve and under eighteen, with her consent and with lewd designs.
t: RA 11648 did not amend this article; it still reads “over twelve and under eighteen”.

article-344.x: Private crimes: adultery and concubinage are prosecuted only upon complaint of the offended spouse, against both guilty parties if alive, and not if he or she consented or pardoned them. Seduction, abduction and acts of lasciviousness need a complaint of the offended party, her parents, grandparents or guardian, and are extinguished by express pardon; marriage of the offender with the offended party extinguishes the action or penalty, also as to co-principals, accomplices and accessories.
t: Rape is no longer a private crime (RA 8353).
The complaint requirement is jurisdictional in the sense that the State cannot proceed without it.
Pardon must come before the institution of the criminal action.

article-345.x: Civil liability in crimes against chastity: indemnifying the offended woman, acknowledging the offspring (unless the law prevents it), and supporting the offspring. In adultery and concubinage, only indemnity.

article-346.x: Ascendants, guardians, curators, teachers and others who, by abuse of authority or confidential relationship, cooperate as accomplices in crimes against chastity are punished as principals.

article-347.x: Simulation of births, substitution of one child for another, and concealment or abandonment of a legitimate child with intent to cause it to lose its civil status; heavier for a public officer or a physician or surgeon who cooperates.
t: RA 11222 (2019) allows rectification of simulated births made before it took effect, without criminal liability, if done for the child’s best interest.

i.s: Persons who simulated a child’s birth before the law took effect, for the child’s best interest, may rectify the record through administrative adoption and are exempt from criminal, civil and administrative liability.

article-348.x: Usurpation of civil status: assuming the civil status of another (e.g., pretending to be a legitimate child or the spouse) to defraud the offended party or his heirs.

article-349.x: Bigamy: contracting a second or subsequent marriage before the first has been legally dissolved, or before the absent spouse has been declared presumptively dead in proper proceedings.
k: The offender is legally married.
The first marriage has not been legally dissolved, or the absent spouse has not been declared presumptively dead.
He or she contracts a second or subsequent marriage.
The second marriage has all the essential requisites for validity (but for the bigamy).
t: Under Art. 40 of the Family Code a judicial declaration of nullity is needed before remarrying. But since Pulido v. People (2021, En Banc), a judicial declaration that the first marriage was void ab initio — even one obtained after the second marriage — is a valid defense.
A voidable first marriage, unannulled, still supports bigamy.
Prescription runs from discovery by the offended spouse or the authorities.

d.h: The Court held that a void ab initio first marriage, judicially declared void even after the second marriage was contracted, is a valid defense in bigamy; it abandoned earlier rulings that required the declaration before the second marriage for purposes of the criminal case.
d.r: The current rule on void first marriages.

article-350.x: Marriage contrary to law: contracting a marriage knowing that the requirements of law were not complied with, or that the marriage is disregarded by a legal impediment (not covered by bigamy); heavier if consent was obtained by violence, intimidation or fraud.

article-352.x: Performance of an illegal marriage ceremony by priests, ministers or civil authorities, punished under the Marriage Law.

article-353.x: Libel: a public and malicious imputation of a crime, a vice or defect (real or imaginary), or any act, omission, condition, status or circumstance tending to cause the dishonor, discredit or contempt of a natural or juridical person, or to blacken the memory of one who is dead.
k: An imputation of a crime, vice, defect, act, omission, condition, status or circumstance.
Publication (communication to a third person).
Identity of the person defamed (identifiable, even if not named).
Malice (presumed from a defamatory imputation, Art. 354).
t: The imputation need not be true or false; truth is a defense only as allowed by Art. 361.
A juridical person, and the memory of the dead, can be defamed.

i.t: Cybercrime Prevention Act (RA 10175), Sec. 4(c)(4) and Sec. 6
i.s: Libel committed through a computer system is cyber libel, punished one degree higher; Disini v. Secretary of Justice (2014) upheld it as to the original author only.
Guidelines in libel cases: courts may, in their discretion, prefer a fine to imprisonment, depending on the circumstances.

article-354.x: Every defamatory imputation is presumed malicious, even if true, unless good intention and justifiable motive are shown, except in privileged communications: (1) a private communication made in the performance of a legal, moral or social duty; (2) a fair and true report, without comments, of official proceedings that are not confidential.
t: In privileged communications, malice is not presumed; the complainant must prove malice in fact.
Fair comment on matters of public interest about public officers and public figures is also protected (actual malice standard for public figures).

article-355.x: Libel by writing, printing, lithography, engraving, radio, phonograph, painting, theatrical exhibition, cinematographic exhibition or similar means: prisión correccional minimum to medium, or a fine (adjusted by RA 10951), or both, besides the civil action.
t: Online libel is cyber libel under RA 10175, one degree higher, and prescribes in one year from discovery (Causing v. People, 2023).

i.t: Cybercrime Prevention Act (RA 10175), Sec. 4(c)(4) and Sec. 6
i.s: Libel committed through a computer system is cyber libel, punished one degree higher; Disini v. Secretary of Justice (2014) upheld it as to the original author only.
Guidelines in libel cases: courts may, in their discretion, prefer a fine to imprisonment, depending on the circumstances.

article-356.x: Threatening to publish a libel concerning a person or his family, or offering to prevent its publication, for compensation (blackmail).

article-357.x: Prohibited publication of acts referred to in the course of official proceedings: a reporter, editor or manager who publishes facts connected with the private life of another that offend his honor, virtue and reputation, even under cover of reporting official proceedings (the “gag law”).

article-358.x: Slander (oral defamation): grave slander — arresto mayor maximum to prisión correccional minimum; otherwise, arresto menor or a fine.
t: Whether slander is grave depends on the words, the parties’ social standing, and the circumstances, including the heat of anger.

article-359.x: Slander by deed: an act that casts dishonor, discredit or contempt upon another in the presence of others (e.g., a slap to humiliate); serious or not, by the nature of the act.
t: If the act is done to cause injury, it is physical injuries or maltreatment (Art. 266); if to dishonor, slander by deed.

article-360.x: Persons responsible and venue (as amended by RA 4363): whoever publishes or causes publication; authors, editors and business managers. Criminal and civil actions for written defamation are filed in the court of the province or city where the libelous article is printed and first published, or where an offended party actually resided at the time (with special rules for public officers); the civil action goes to the same court.
t: Venue in libel is jurisdictional in criminal cases: the information must allege the facts that establish it.
Courts of First Instance are now the Regional Trial Courts, which have exclusive original jurisdiction over libel.

article-361.x: Proof of truth: truth is admissible and acquits if the imputation was published with good motives and justifiable ends; truth of an imputed crime is a defense, but truth of other imputations is a defense only when the offended party is a public officer and the act relates to official duties.

article-362.x: Libelous remarks or comments connected with privileged matter (Art. 354) are not exempt if made with malice.

article-363.x: Incriminating an innocent person: performing an act (not perjury) that directly incriminates or imputes to an innocent person the commission of a crime (planting evidence).
t: If done through false testimony, the crime is perjury or false testimony; planting of drugs or firearms is also punished by special laws (RA 9165, Sec. 29; RA 10591).

article-364.x: Intriguing against honor: any intrigue whose principal purpose is to blemish the honor or reputation of a person, when it is not libel or slander (e.g., spreading gossip whose source cannot be traced).

article-365.x: Imprudence and negligence: reckless imprudence (voluntary act, without malice, from inexcusable lack of precaution) and simple imprudence (lack of precaution where the damage is not immediate or the danger not clearly manifest). The penalty depends on whether the act, if intentional, would be a grave, less grave or light felony; failure to help the injured on the spot raises it.
k: Reckless imprudence: (1) a voluntary act; (2) without malice; (3) material damage results; (4) from inexcusable lack of precaution, considering the person’s employment, intelligence, physical condition and other circumstances.
Simple imprudence: the damage impending is not immediate, or the danger not clearly manifest.
t: Reckless imprudence is a single crime: its several consequences (homicide, injuries, damage) do not make several offenses. A conviction or acquittal for one consequence bars prosecution for the others (Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro).
The court is not bound by the rules of Art. 64 in fixing the penalty.

d.h: Reckless imprudence is a distinct crime, not a mode of committing other crimes; a driver convicted of reckless imprudence resulting in slight physical injuries could not be tried again for reckless imprudence resulting in homicide and damage to property from the same act (double jeopardy).

article-366.x: Felonies committed before the Code took effect are punished under the laws then in force, without prejudice to Art. 22 (retroactivity of penal laws favorable to the accused).

article-367.x: Repealing clause: the old Penal Code, the Provisional Law, and the Acts listed are repealed, except as provided in Art. 366.
